B-GRTO: Bootstrapped Group Relative Tool Optimization for Referring Segmentation

Mario Markov†    Stefan Maria Ailuro    Mohammad Mahdi Affiliation: Luc Van Gool,  Danda Pani Paudel Affiliation: INSAIT, Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski” Email: †mario.markov@insait.ai
Abstract

Segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, underpinning pixel-level scene understanding and serving as a cornerstone for applications ranging from autonomous perception to medical image analysis. For complex referring segmentation, recent methods pair large vision-language models with segmentation decoders: the former analyzes the image and prompt, while the latter predicts the target mask. Although reinforcement learning improves reasoning-intensive vision-language systems, trainable tools such as segmentation decoders are typically optimized separately with differentiable objectives, and the principled integration of such objectives into reinforcement learning remains underexplored. Thus, we introduce group relative tool optimization (GRTO), a mathematically grounded framework for jointly optimizing a policy with differentiable tool use. GRTO reuses group relative policy optimization (GRPO) rollouts to optimize the auxiliary tool objective, letting decoder gradients complement policy rewards. Further, we derive Bootstrapped-GRTO (B-GRTO), a pretraining method that cheaply bootstraps the tool, leading to faster convergence and superior performance. Across three challenging referring segmentation settings, B-GRTO results in substantial improvements over plain GRPO, matching or surpassing domain-specific state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates the value of unifying reinforcement learning with differentiable auxiliary objectives for reasoning-intensive segmentation.

1 Introduction

Referring segmentation tasks require a model to produce a pixel-level mask for a target specified by natural language. Unlike conventional semantic segmentation, where each pixel is assigned to one of a fixed set of predefined categories, referring segmentation conditions the output on an open-ended prompt. Flexible target descriptions are central to open-ended visual interfaces, robotics, medical image analysis, safety-critical perception, and open-world perception, where segmentation should follow intent rather than fixed categories [3, 9, 65]. However, in challenging cases, the prompt may initially be ambiguous or under-specified. Then, the model needs to determine which object is being referred to before it can segment. The task therefore combines dense mask prediction with prompt disambiguation.

Existing methods tend to address these two problems separately. When the segmentation decoder is insufficient for a target domain, it is trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to improve mask quality. This is effective when the object to segment is already well specified, but it does not solve cases where the prompt itself requires nontrivial interpretation. Interpreting difficult prompts also requires world knowledge and the ability to connect language in context to high-level visual semantics. This motivates systems that combine dense segmentation decoders with multimodal large-language models (MLLMs). Their representations are better suited to resolve the complex, nonlocal, and compositional reasoning needed to determine what should be segmented [12, 15, 25]. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural way to optimize the reasoning policy because the desired intermediate interpretation is rarely annotated. Training data usually provides only the final mask, not the disentangled prompt representation. RL can improve the MLLM using final-mask rewards, letting it explore prompt alternative interpretations and reinforce those yielding better masks [31, 32, 66]. However, existing RL-based approaches typically update the MLLM while keeping the segmentation decoder fixed. This ignores differentiable tool feedback that could adapt the decoder to the same successful episodes guiding the policy.

This reveals an important underexplored setting: referring segmentation where both sources of difficulty are present at the same time. In many realistic applications, the prompt is not fully explicit and the visual domain is also challenging. A remote-sensing user may ask for “heaven for sunbathers and swimmers” while a camouflage dataset may require identifying the “camouflaged object.” Such cases require both referring-expression reasoning and adaptation to subtle, domain-specific visual cues. Improving only reasoning leaves mask quality decoder-limited; improving only the decoder assumes the target is known. A method for this setting must therefore jointly optimize the reasoning policy and the segmentation tool, as outlined in Figure 1. More generally, this is an instance of trainable tool use: when a reasoning policy calls a tool, policy-level rewards need not be the only learning signal.

However, this joint optimization is asymmetric: the policy is large and costly to improve through action sampling, whereas the tool is often lightweight and cheaply updated with differentiable objectives. This suggests that effective methods should exploit cheaper opportunities to pre-align and refine the tool before reinforcement learning. Crucially, such pre-alignment should not merely fit the tool to the behavior of the initial policy; it must anticipate and support the policy after training, so that the tool remains aligned with the improved reasoning strategy that reinforcement learning is expected to produce.

We introduce bootstrapped group relative tool optimization (B-GRTO), a framework for jointly optimizing a reasoning policy and trainable differentiable tool within group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [52], without limiting tool training to policy-optimization speed. B-GRTO has two stages: bootstrapped tool optimization (BTO), which cheaply pre-aligns the tool to the theoretical post-trained policy, and group relative tool optimization (GRTO), which integrates tool fine-tuning into policy RL. We evaluate B-GRTO on three challenging settings in the referring segmentation domain: remote sensing segmentation, camouflaged object detection, and reasoning segmentation, where it delivers substantial gains over conventional policy-only GRPO, competing with in-domain state-of-the-art (SoTA) architectures.

2 Related works

Multimodal LLMs for Language-Instructed Segmentation.

Early approaches to language-guided segmentation tightly couple a large language model with a pixel decoder via special segmentation token [25, 62, 23, 58, 47, 60, 55] into the LLM’s vocabulary whose embedding is decoded by SAM [24] into a binary mask. Several designs substitute the token with a full code-book [49, 68] or a separate text encoder [36]. A common limitation across this entire family is that all components are optimized with standard cross-entropy on fixed annotation sets, which can overfit to the label distribution, limiting generalization, and does not allow the model to explore novel approaches that could lead to superior results.

Decoder as a tool and Reinforcement Learning.

The success of group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [52] for reasoning in language models has given rise to a second generation of segmentation approaches that use it to learn robust and accurate tool-use of SAM [48]. Earlier versions use it only as a test-time tool, training on bounding-box IoU rewards [6, 31, 32, 72]. Later works introduce tool-use at training to access end-to-end mask IoU rewards [21, 66]. Several methods suggest tool-prompting in latent space, trained with a segmentation loss [73, 37], and attempts are made to employ these methods in specialized domains, e.g. in remote sensing [63, 67] or pathology [33]. Further, agentic setups with multi-turn tool-use are also investigated with promising results [2, 10, 18, 74]. These approaches demonstrate that RL-refined language actions reasoning measurably lift segmentation quality even when the segmentation tool itself is held fixed. However, most of the methods practically assume SAM to be a perfect tool and do not explore the potential gain in treating SAM as a trainable component.

SAM Fine-Tuning for Specialized Domains.

Although SAM exhibits strong zero-shot segmentation capabilities, its performance degrades on out-of-distribution imagery. Fine-tuning SAM on well-camouflaged animals, cast shadows, and medical images is shown to substantially recover accuracy in these failure modes [4]. Analogously, in remote sensing, fine-tuned SAM variants outperform prompt-tuned baselines on building footprints, solar panels, sinkholes, and dead-tree detection [1]. However, these studies assume perfect prompts, whereas in real-world scenarios prompts are often ambiguous or too long to be tokenized by SAM.

Motivated by these limitations, we study referring segmentation as a trainable tool-use problem in which both the reasoning policy and the segmentation decoder may need to adapt. Rather than treating the decoder as a fixed reward component or fine-tuning it independently under perfectly specified prompts, we propose B-GRTO: a two-stage framework that first bootstraps the tool toward rollouts expected to be reinforced, and then jointly optimizes the policy and tool within GRPO (Figure 2).

3 Method

Preliminary. We seek to optimize the standard KL-regularized RL objective [54, 46, 52] for policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, with a parametrized tool ψω\psi_{\omega} and reward RR:

JKL-RL(θ,ω)=𝔼πθ[R(ψω)]−βDKL(πθ||πθ0),J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[R(\psi_{\omega})]-\beta\,\text{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}||\pi_{\theta_{0}}), (1)

where policy and tool are initialized from reference models πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} and ψω0\psi_{\omega_{0}}.

Commonly, in RL with tool-use one only trains the policy model, keeping the tool fixed:

θ0↦argmaxθJKL-RL​(θ,ω0),ω0↦ω0,\theta_{0}\mapsto\argmax_{\theta}J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega_{0}),\quad\omega_{0}\mapsto\omega_{0}, (2)

To solve it for θ\theta, one employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [7, 35], where a group of rollouts {o1..oG}∼πo​l​d\{o_{1}..o_{G}\}\sim\pi_{old} is sampled from the policy at the current optimization step, the mean μ\mu of rewards {R1..RG}\{R_{1}..R_{G}\} is used as a baseline for the policy gradient, and their standard deviation σ\sigma is used as normalization for numerical stability:

JGRPO(θ,ω0)=1G∑i=1G∑t=1|oi|min(ri,tAi,clip(ri,t,1−ε,1+ε)Ai)−βDKL(πθ||πθ0),ri,t=πθ​(oi,t|oi,<t)πo​l​d​(oi,t|oi,<t),Ai=Ri−μσ,\displaystyle\begin{split}J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta,\omega_{0})=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}&\min(r_{i,t}\,A_{i},\texttt{clip}(r_{i,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{i})-\beta\,\text{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}||\pi_{\theta_{0}}),\\ r_{i,t}&=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{old}(o_{i,t}|o_{i,<t})},\quad A_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu}{\sigma},\end{split} (3)

Here ψω0\psi_{\omega_{0}} is treated as part of the reward model, and it is usually assumed that ω0\omega_{0} is already sufficient for downstream performance. While this assumption holds in some cases like code execution, it is not guaranteed for complex parametrized tools derived from an optimization process of their own.

Joint Optimization. When the tool ψω\psi_{\omega} is a pretrained model, it may under-perform under domain shifts [1, 4]. Moreover, one may treat (θ,ω)(\theta,\,\omega) as the single set of weights of the unified model, and in that case it is beneficial to allow them to align with each other during optimization. Therefore, our goal is to maximize a joint objective:

(θ0,ω0)↦argmax(θ,ω)JKL-RL​(θ,ω)(\theta_{0},\,\omega_{0})\mapsto\argmax_{(\theta,\,\omega)}J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega) (4)

For policy gradient we use JGRPOJ_{\text{GRPO}} (3) with rewards calculated using current tool parameters ωold\omega_{\text{old}}; and to estimate the tool gradient we reuse the sampled group of rollouts from πo​l​d\pi_{old}:

∇θJKL-RL≈∇θJGRPO(θ,ωold),∇ωJKL-RL=𝔼πθ∇ωR(ψω)≈−1G∑i=1G∏t=1|oi|ri,t∇ωℒ(ψω)\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{KL-RL}}\approx\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta,\omega_{\text{old}}),\quad\nabla_{\omega}J_{\text{KL-RL}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\nabla_{\omega}R(\psi_{\omega})\approx-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\prod_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}r_{i,t}\nabla_{\omega}\mathcal{L}(\psi_{\omega}) (5)

where the gradient of the reward is approximated with the gradient of a surrogate loss function ℒ\mathcal{L}.

In order to achieve unified policy and tool optimization (4) we define the group relative tool optimization (GRTO) objective:

JGRTO​(θ,ω)=JGRPO​(θ,ωold)−1G​∑i=1G∏t=1|oi|ri,t′​ℒ​(ψω)J_{\text{GRTO}}(\theta,\omega)=J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta,\omega_{\text{old}})-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\prod_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}r^{\prime}_{i,t}\mathcal{L}(\psi_{\omega}) (6)

Where ri,t′=stopgrad​(ri,t)r^{\prime}_{i,t}=\text{stopgrad}(r_{i,t}) and the reward function RR are treated as non-differentiable in order to reconstruct the gradients (5).

Bootstrapping the Tool. A practical bottleneck in joint GRTO training is matching training velocities: ψω\psi_{\omega} is often a lightweight deterministic module that can be evaluated and updated cheaply, but during GRTO it can only be updated as fast as πθ\pi_{\theta} whose rollouts and updates are often vastly more expensive. This asymmetry suggests a natural bootstrapping strategy to first pretrain the tool using a fixed replay buffer of rollouts [14]. A better-conditioned tool should also provide a more reliable reward signal during the second stage, thereby improving the stability and convergence of policy optimization. The challenge is formulating the pretraining objective to be consistent with JKL-RLJ_{\text{KL-RL}} (1).

To achieve the consistent objective, we employ a known Bayesian-posterior policy πθ∗​(ω)\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)} [54] which, for β>0\beta>0 and a fixed ω\omega, maximizes JKL-RLJ_{\text{KL-RL}} (1):

πθ∗​(ω)=1Zω​πθ0​e1β​R​(ψω),Zω=𝔼πθ0​[e1β​R​(ψω)]\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}=\frac{1}{Z_{\omega}}\pi_{\theta_{0}}\,e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R(\psi_{\omega})},\quad Z_{\omega}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta_{0}}}\left[e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R(\psi_{\omega})}\right] (7)
maxω,θ⁡JKL-RL​(θ,ω)=maxω⁡maxθ​JKL-RL​(θ,ω)=maxω⁡JKL-RL​(θ∗​(ω),ω)\max_{\omega,\theta}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega)=\max_{\omega}\,\max_{\theta}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega)=\max_{\omega}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta^{*}(\omega),\omega) (8)

where ZωZ_{\omega} is a constant ensuring that πθ∗​(ω)\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)} is a valid normalized probability distribution. Thus, the optimization problem can be solved for tool parameters ω\omega independently, using groups sampled from the reference policy {o1..oG}∼πθ0\{o_{1}..o_{G}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}. This yields our bootstrapped tool optimization (BTO) objective:

JBTO(ω)=−1G∑i=1G1Ze1β​Riℒ(ψω),Z=∑i=1Ge1β​RiJ_{\text{BTO}}(\omega)=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{Z}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R_{i}}\mathcal{L}(\psi_{\omega}),\quad Z=\sum_{i=1}^{G}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R_{i}} (9)

where ZZ and the reward function RR are treated as non-differentiable. For the detailed derivation, see Appendix B.

However, as this uses crude approximations of an idealized πθ∗\pi_{\theta^{*}}, the bootstrapped tool would not perfectly align with the learned policy. Therefore, we still apply GRTO as a second training stage to train θ\theta and further fine-tune ω\omega.

Overall, we propose Bootstrapped-GRTO (B-GRTO) consisting of two stages:

(θ0,ω0)↦(θ0,argmaxωJBTO​(ω))↦argmax(θ,ω)JGRTO​(θ,ω)(\theta_{0},\omega_{0})\mapsto(\theta_{0},\argmax_{\omega}J_{\text{BTO}}(\omega))\mapsto\argmax_{(\theta,\,\omega)}J_{\text{GRTO}}(\theta,\omega) (10)

where the preconditioned tool at the second stage should facilitate convergence. For method overview, see Figure 3

B-GRTO in referring segmentation. In our setting, the policy is InternVL3.5-8B [56], which generates concise noun phrases and bounding boxes for the referred object instances. These concepts and boxes are parsed as prompts for SAM3 [2] in promptable concept segmentation mode, producing segmentation masks conditioned on the image and generated prompts. Finally, we apply deterministic spatial filtering by setting all pixels outside the generated boxes to background, so the boxes serve as both prompts and hard spatial constraints.

4 Experiments

We select InternVL3.5-8B as our VLM backbone across experiments due to its strong performance across various domains and tasks including visual grounding [56], and SAM3 as our mask generator [2]. We optimize SAM3 using a differentiable BCE + soft-IoU surrogate, while evaluating the VLM with final-mask IoU as the reward signal. For the detailed experimental setup, see Appendix E. We conduct experiments on three challenging referring segmentation settings:

Camouflage detection. Camouflaged objects commonly exhibit much lower contrast and higher appearance similarity to their surroundings compared to common segmentation targets. COD10K [13] and CAMO [26] are widely used camouflaged object segmentation benchmarks with pixel-level object mask annotations. As these datasets do not provide a separate validation split, a recent line of work has started using the testing set as validation set [4, 70, 61]. We instead follow the protocol of splitting the training set into train and validation subsets, and compare with the SoTA within that protocol [22]. We report standard camouflaged object detection metrics: S-measure, weighted F-measure, E-measure, and mean absolute error. We select checkpoints with the highest validation weighted F-measure. In line with previous works, we also benchmark final models zero-shot on a third camouflage detection dataset: NC4K [38].

Recent COD methods add task-specific priors to generic segmentation architectures, including boundary enhancement [17, 71, 22], frequency or wavelet features [53, 61], multi-scale context [45, 42], and foreground–background contrast or saliency disambiguation [22]. These designs reflect the need to recover subtle object boundaries and separate low-contrast camouflaged regions from visually similar backgrounds.

Remote sensing segmentation. Unlike natural images, remote sensing imagery typically captures expansive scenes with dense, repetitive structures and objects spanning widely varying scales. EarthReason [27] is a large-scale geospatial pixel reasoning benchmark comprising manually annotated image masks and implicit question-answer pairs for evaluating reasoning-guided remote sensing segmentation. We use it to train, test and evaluate in this setting. In line with current SoTA in this setting [67], we report gIoU and cIoU: the average of per-sample IoUs, and the cumulative intersection over cumulative union.

Prior geospatial reasoning segmentation methods use remote-sensing-specific designs such as visual token compression, multi-scale language–vision fusion, spatial-correlation-aware mask generation, and task transformations for object-, region-, and pixel-level outputs [27, 63]. These adaptations address common properties of overhead imagery, including large spatial extent, small dense objects, and heterogeneous scene layouts.

Challenging reasoning segmentation. Challenging reasoning segmentation requires grounding targets from complex queries involving compositional, relational, contextual, or world-knowledge reasoning. ReasonSeg-X and ReasonSeg-R [66] are recently introduced benchmarks designed to stress-test reasoning-driven segmentation beyond standard referring expressions. ReasonSeg-R refines the original ReasonSeg benchmark [25], providing test samples with corrected annotation and query issues. ReasonSeg-X extends the task with harder samples that require deeper and more systematic reasoning. Similarly to the current SoTA, we first pretrain the base model on common reasoning segmentation datasets before conducting the full range of experiments [66]. Following prior work, we report gIoU and cIoU.

Recent SoTA methods for challenging reasoning segmentation invest additional computation directly into the reasoning process. In particular, StAR uses parallel test-time scaling through mask-level majority voting over multiple stochastic reasoning traces, effectively aggregating diverse candidate localizations before producing the final mask [66]. Its rollout-expanded selective tuning samples 128–256 trajectories but updates only on informative high- and low-advantage responses, mitigating weak signals when most rollouts are incorrect or uninformative.

For the complete prompts across all experiments, see Appendix G.

4.1 Experimental configurations

Main experiments. For each of the three settings, we train three configurations: standard GRPO, where we only fine-tune InternVL3.5, treating SAM3 as a frozen auxiliary tool; GRTO where we backpropagate the differentiable loss on SAM3 during GRPO as defined in Section 3; and Bootstrapped-GRTO (B-GRTO), where we pretrain SAM3 by pre-generating groups of rollouts with the reference policy once and backpropagating the objective in (9) on SAM3 until validation performance peaks, and proceed with standard GRTO training afterwards. In B-GRTO bootstrapping, we use experience replay [14]: rollout groups are generated once, stored, and treated as a static fine-tuning dataset. Its overhead is comparable to a single GRPO epoch, since after groups are rolled out once, the computational cost of fine-tuning SAM3 is comparatively negligible.

Ablations. We perform two ablations to probe different training and inference regimes, conducted in the remote sensing setting, as experiments are least expensive there. The sequential training implied by B-GRTO, as derived in Section 3, should in practice produce a better aligned decoder. To verify this, we examine a different sequential training regime: first train the policy with GRPO, and after convergence, fine-tune SAM3 on deterministic policy outputs. In theory, this also produces a decoder aligned with the VLM, but not with the theoretical common objective. We call this regime Reverse-Sequential. To assess the post-filtering procedure described at the end of Section 3, we also evaluate GRTO without setting pixels outside predicted boxes to background. We refer to this ablation as GRTO-No-Filter. Finally, we ablate a third regime: fine-tune the tool with BTO, then perform GRPO instead of second-stage joint optimization. This is potentially valuable in memory-bound settings where the policy and tool cannot be trained jointly. We call this Bootstrapped-GRPO (B-GRPO), and perform the experiment in the remote-sensing and camouflage detection settings.

4.2 Results

Refer to Tables 1, 2(a), and 2(b) for the complete results of the main experiments. See Figure 4 for ablation results.

Camouflage detection. In camouflage detection, GRTO substantially improves over GRPO, and B-GRTO performs best across all metrics. B-GRTO reaches state-of-the-art performance on COD10K and NC4K, ranking top-two across all metrics, and remains near state-of-the-art on CAMO, ranking top-five across all metrics.

Remote sensing segmentation. In EarthReason, GRTO and B-GRTO once again significantly enhance plain-GRPO. In this setting, GRTO is slightly better than B-GRTO; however, B-GRTO has superior convergence (refer to Appendix C). All our configurations, including plain GRPO, outperform the previous SoTA that also uses a VLM-conditioned SAM with different backbones and conditioning protocol [67].

Challenging reasoning segmentation. Within the in-domain dataset ReasonSeg-X, GRTO and B-GRTO consistently beat the GRPO baseline. However, in the zero-shot setting, the results are more nuanced: B-GRTO competes with GRPO, whereas GRTO demonstrates substantially worse performance. Overall, B-GRTO achieves the highest number of first-place rankings among the evaluated configurations. Compared to StAR Qwen 3, the current SoTA in this setting [66], neither of our configurations ranks in the top two. However, relative to the stage-1 model, reported only for their Qwen 2.5 backbone, B-GRTO yields a substantially larger gain, even over their majority-voting (MV) inference strategy. This is notable because our stage-1 model is comparable to, and slightly weaker than, StAR Qwen 2.5.

Ablations. In the remote sensing ablations, Reverse-Sequential does not match GRTO, the best-performing configuration. The bounding-box filtering protocol also has a clear impact, as removing it degrades performance. Finally, B-GRPO shows that BTO effectively bootstraps the tool in camouflage and remote sensing even without joint training, substantially improving over GRPO; nevertheless, B-GRTO remains strongest overall.

5 Discussion

Fine-tuning the decoder is important, but it must be aligned with the policy objective. An important empirical lesson from our experiments is that the segmentation decoder should not be treated as a passive implementation detail. Even if the language model improves grounding, final masks remain limited by the decoder’s ability to handle noisy, partial, or domain-shifted prompts. Across all configurations we test, fine-tuning SAM3 yields substantial performance gains – even in the theoretically misaligned Reverse-Sequential ablation (see Section 4.1). This is also visible in Figure 1 and Appendix D: in camouflage detection, the decoder excludes fine-grained occlusions; in remote sensing, it adapts to dataset-specific annotation semantics not expressible through the conditioning mechanism; and in reasoning segmentation, it better delineates small or scattered objects. Decoder fine-tuning is most effective when it is aligned with the direction of policy optimization: reverse-Sequential also fine-tunes the decoder, but because it is not aligned with the joint objective derived in Section 3, it fails to surpass GRTO. Qualitatively, GRTO and B-GRTO improve not only the decoder but also the VLM’s tool-use behavior, leading it to produce more descriptive and concise prompts. This is clearest for B-GRTO, where a pre-aligned tool steers the VLM toward better conditioning and enables better convergence (see Appendix C). GRTO-No-Filter further supports this interpretation: removing VLM-based mask post-filtering degrades performance, suggesting that GRTO learns complementary policy–tool behaviors whose benefits depend on coordinated use.

Bootstrapping enables cheaper and more effective optimization. We use a minimal bootstrapping strategy: populate the replay buffer once with one or two rollout epochs, then fine-tune the tool on this static dataset using the Section 3 objective. Even this minimal procedure yields clear gains in convergence and final performance, and the B-GRPO ablation (Section 4.1) shows that using only the bootstrapped tool during GRPO already yields a more robust system. This enables practical applications of our method even when resources are insufficient for joint training. However, B-GRPO does not replace GRTO: as the policy improves, its prompt distribution may drift from the fixed bootstrapping buffer. Joint optimization can keep adapting the decoder to this evolving distribution, leading to the best empirical results.

B-GRTO as a general-purpose method. Across experiments, B-GRTO remains competitive with SoTA methods using domain-tailored architectural priors (Section 4). The main exception is reasoning segmentation, where our model does not reach the absolute top performance. However, this setting is sensitive to first-stage pretraining: following prior work [66], we pretrain on a small single-pass sample from a large dataset mixture (Sections 4 and E), introducing variance from the sampled subset and backbone. As shown in Table 2(b), our stage-1 model starts below the reported StAR Qwen 2.5 backbone. Even so, GRTO and B-GRTO yield larger gains than StAR obtains on Qwen 2.5 with its training procedure and inference protocol, which require significantly more policy rollouts. This positions B-GRTO as a general-purpose approach for competitive cross-domain performance, combining MLLM representations with adaptable tools without domain-specific architectures or expensive test-time aggregation.

Limitations. As with any training method, GRTO and B-GRTO run the risk of overfitting the decoder to the dataset at hand. This appears in reasoning segmentation, where the training set has only 240 samples (Section 4) and GRTO’s best checkpoint after 11 epochs (Figure 7) shows degraded zero-shot performance. This is not the case for B-GRTO, whose selected checkpoint is at epoch 6. Additionally, the bootstrapping stage depends on the quality and diversity of the initial replay buffer. If the reference policy almost never generates useful prompts for a class of examples, then BTO has limited signal for those cases. Increasing group size and sampling variance can mitigate this issue, but it increases rollout cost and storage. More adaptive replay strategies, such as refreshing the buffer after partial policy improvement or mixing reference and current-policy rollouts, may improve robustness. Finally, during hyperparameter search, we observe that the system is sensitive to mismatched learning rates between the policy and the tool. B-GRTO must therefore be applied with care, and hyperparameters should be carefully calibrated.

Future work. In this paper, we use a deliberately simple static replay buffer, yet the resulting bootstrapped tools already improve robustness and, in several settings, lead to superior final performance. This suggests that more adaptive bootstrapping procedures may yield further gains. Potential directions are dynamic replay buffers refreshed as the policy improves, curricula for difficult or underrepresented examples, or hybrid buffers mixing reference- and intermediate-policy rollouts. Although costlier, such strategies may provide more diverse, higher-quality tool supervision, yielding a more robust decoder and stronger rewards during joint optimization. More broadly, these results indicate that investing additional computation in tool bootstrapping could be a practical way to improve final performance, especially in settings where stable tool behavior is critical for effective policy learning.

6 Conclusion

We present B-GRTO, a framework for aligning a reasoning policy with a differentiable tool. GRTO uses GRPO rollouts for both reward-based policy learning and importance-weighted tool fine-tuning, while B-GRTO cheaply bootstraps the tool to improve rewards and enhance joint optimization.

Across camouflage detection, remote sensing segmentation, and challenging reasoning segmentation, fine-tuning the decoder improves over policy-only GRPO. B-GRTO is strongest overall, achieving the best final performance in two of three settings and fastest convergence in two of three settings. Further, our method establishes state-of-the-art performance in camouflage detection and remote sensing segmentation, while also providing strong gains on challenging reasoning segmentation.

These results show that trainable tools should not be treated as fixed reward components in reasoning-intensive segmentation. Instead, aligning the tool with the policy objective yields stronger, faster, and more robust optimization, making B-GRTO a general strategy for combining MLLM reasoning with adaptable differentiable tools.

Appendix A Extended Related Works

Multimodal LLMs for Language-Instructed Segmentation.

Early approaches to language-guided segmentation tightly couple a large language model with a pixel decoder via special segmentation tokens. LISA [25] introduce this paradigm, appending a single <SEG> token to the LLM’s vocabulary whose embedding is decoded by SAM [24] into a binary mask.

Subsequent work extends LISA along several axes: LISA++ [62] and M2SA [23] handle multiple objects per query, and SegLLM [58] enable multi-turn conversational grounding. GLaMM [47] enrich this design with grounded captions and region-level understanding, while GSVA [60] incorporate rejection mechanisms for queries that lack a valid referent. X-SAM [55] further generalizes the architecture toward open-vocabulary and versatile segmentation.

Several designs beyond a <SEG> token are explored. RSVP [36] substitutes it with a BEiT-3-encoder [57] over object tokens pre-detected by a MLLM. PixelLM [49] replaces it with a learned code-book of pixel embeddings for multi-target settings, and PSALM [68] adds rejection handling to it.

A common limitation across this entire family is that all components are optimized with standard cross-entropy on fixed annotation sets, which can overfit to the label distribution, limiting generalization, and does not allow the model to explore novel approaches that could lead to superior results.

Decoder as a tool and Reinforcement Learning.

SAM4LLM [6] is one of the first to train an MLLM to output bounding-boxes to prompt a frozen SAM2 [48], using it as an external tool. While they used supervised fine-tuning (SFT), the success of group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [52] for reasoning in language models has inspired a second generation of segmentation approaches that use it to learn robust and accurate tool-use of SAM.

Seg-Zero [31] pioneer this regime, training the reasoning VLM with bounding-box IoU rewards, and using SAM itself only at inference. VisionReasoner [32] and POPEN [72] extend Seg-Zero’s multi-object handling, with POPEN using DPO [46] on top of a LISA-pretrained backbone. SAM-R1 [21] and StAR [66] extend the approach to end-to-end rewards, evaluating SAM during training and using its mask IoU as reward. LENS [73] and CoRPS [37] suggest changing the prompting approach by adding a learnable context encoder and a correlation prior, respectively. To train introduced modules, they backpropagate a segmentation loss while tuning a MLLM with GRPO under mask-IoU rewards. Several attempts are made to employ these methods for specialized domains, e.g. RemoteReasoner [63] and Think2Seg [67] in the remote sensing domain, or PathChat-SegR1[33] in the pathology domain.

SAM3 agent [2] suggests interacting with the segmentation decoder in a multi-turn, agentic manner. SAM-Veteran [10] improves these interactions by multi-turn GRPO training, rewarding both mask and box quality across dialogue turns. RSAgent [18] improves it further by adding agentic perception. SegAgent [74] explores a complementary agent formulation using Tree-of-Thoughts planning and a hybrid RL/SFT objective, enabling iterative mask refinement without gradient flow through SAM.

These approaches demonstrate that RL-shaped language reasoning measurably lifts segmentation quality even when the segmentation tool itself is held fixed. However, most of the methods practically assume SAM to be a perfect tool and do not explore the potential gain in treating SAM as a trainable component.

SAM Fine-Tuning for Specialized Domains.

Although SAM exhibits strong zero-shot segmentation capabilities, its performance degrades on out-of-distribution imagery. Fine-tuning SAM on well-camouflaged animals, cast shadows, and medical images is shown to substantially recover accuracy in these failure modes [4]. Analogously, in remote sensing, fine-tuned SAM variants outperform prompt-tuned baselines on building footprints, solar panels, sinkholes, and dead-tree detection [1]. However, these studies assume perfect prompts, whereas in real-world scenarios prompts are often ambiguous or too long to be tokenized by SAM.

These findings motivate our joint fine-tuning of SAM 3 alongside the language backbone.

Joint RL for dense outputs beyond segmentation.

The composition of vision-language understanding and dense generation has been studied beyond segmentation. FireScope [41] attaches a U-Net [50] decoder to a reasoning model to generate wildfire risk maps, the MLLM and decoder are trained in stages with GRPO and regression loss respectively. Janus [59, 5] interleave visual understanding and image generation within a single autoregressive transformer with a joint vocabulary. Several works [11, 44, 39] have applied GRPO to the Janus architecture for joint reasoning and image generation. Bagel [8] similarly unite language tokens with normalization flows trained by flow matching for language-instructed image-to-image tasks. Several approaches [30, 64] apply RL to Bagel with summed objectives of text GRPO and Flow-GRPO [29].

While these methods target generation rather than segmentation, they support the general finding that joint fine-tuning improves the quality of language-instructed dense outputs.

maxω,θ⁡JKL-RL​(θ,ω)=maxω⁡maxθ​JKL-RL​(θ,ω)=maxω⁡JKL-RL​(θ∗​(ω),ω)\max_{\omega,\theta}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega)=\max_{\omega}\,\max_{\theta}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta,\omega)=\max_{\omega}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta^{*}(\omega),\omega) (12)

where ZωZ_{\omega} is a constant ensuring that πθ∗​(ω)\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)} is a valid normalized probability distribution. Thus, the optimization problem can be solved for tool parameters ω\omega independently:

JKL-RL​(θ∗​(ω),ω)=𝔼πθ∗​(ω)​[R⁡(ψω)−β​log⁡(πθ∗​(ω)πθ0)]==𝔼πθ∗​(ω)[R⁡(ψω)−β​log⁡(1Zω​e1β​R​(ψω))]=maxω⁡𝔼πθ∗​(ω)​[β​log​Zω]=β​log​Zω\displaystyle\begin{split}&J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta^{*}(\omega),\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}}\left[R(\psi_{\omega})-\beta\,\log\left(\frac{\pi_{{\theta^{*}(\omega)}}}{\pi_{\theta_{0}}}\right)\right]=\\ =\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}}&\left[R(\psi_{\omega})-\beta\,\log\left(\frac{1}{Z_{\omega}}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R(\psi_{\omega})}\right)\right]=\max_{\omega}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}}[\beta\log Z_{\omega}]=\beta\log Z_{\omega}\end{split} (13)

Analyzing its gradients and substituting the gradient of the reward with the gradient of a surrogate loss ℒ\mathcal{L} as in (5):

∇ωJKL-RL(θ∗(ω),ω)=(∇ωβlogZω)=β1Zω∇ωZω≈−1G∑i=1G1Ze1β​Ri∇ωℒs​e​g(ψω)\nabla_{\omega}\,J_{\text{KL-RL}}(\theta^{*}(\omega),\omega)=\left(\nabla_{\omega}\,\beta\log Z_{\omega}\right)=\beta\frac{1}{Z_{\omega}}\nabla_{\omega}Z_{\omega}\approx-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{Z}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R_{i}}\nabla_{\omega}\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\psi_{\omega}) (14)

where the group is sampled from the reference policy {o1..oG}∼πθ0\{o_{1}..o_{G}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}. We define the bootstrapped tool optimization (BTO) objective:

JBTO(ω)=−1G∑i=1G1Ze1β​Riℒ(ψω),Z=∑i=1Ge1β​RiJ_{\text{BTO}}(\omega)=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{Z}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R_{i}}\mathcal{L}(\psi_{\omega}),\quad Z=\sum_{i=1}^{G}e^{\frac{1}{\beta}R_{i}} (15)

where the reward function RR and ZZ are treated as non-differentiable.

Noticing the striking similarity between BTO and the second term of the GRTO objective (6), the gradients of BTO can be viewed as tool gradients in GRTO in an extreme off-policy setting, assuming θ→θ∗\theta\rightarrow\theta^{*} and θo​l​d→θ0\theta_{old}\rightarrow\theta_{0}, with importance sampling weights πθ∗πθ0\frac{\pi_{\theta^{*}}}{\pi_{\theta_{0}}}.

Appendix E Detailed experimental setup

Across all experiments, we fine-tune SAM3’s semantic mask decoder, keeping the rest of the model frozen. We use intersection over union (IoU) as our GRPO reward with only a small validity component to encourage valid output formats, without supervising intermediate conditioning to allow the VLM to freely discover the most optimal conditioning strategy. To train the tool with a differentiable reward surrogate, we combine soft-IoU with pixel-wise binary cross-entropy (BCE) between the predicted foreground mask and the ground-truth foreground mask. Detailed descriptions of reward and loss are available below. Both primarily encourage overlap between the predicted and target masks. We conduct each experiment on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs for up to 30 hours. Across all experiments, we set the KL-divergence weight β=0.01\beta=0.01, and we use a validation set to evaluate on every epoch. We train until validation performance peaks, and benchmark the best validation checkpoint.

Remote sensing and camouflage detection. In the remote sensing and camouflage detection settings, We use a global batch size of 64 unique prompts per batch and a group size of 8, amounting to a total of 512 generations per batch. We set the maximum output length to 1024 tokens. For the bootstrapping stage, our experience replay consists of 8 generations per group. In the remote sensing setting, where the training set has six unique prompts for every image, one epoch consists of one randomly sampled prompt per image for robustness during training. We use a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} for InternVL3.5 across all trainings, and a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for SAM3 for all trainings except second-stage B-GRTO for remote sensing where we set SAM3’s learning rate to 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, because the dynamic epochs already yield a nearly converged model. We train for 12 epoch on remote sensing and 9 epochs on camouflage. We perform full-model training on the VLM.

For camouflage detection, we separate 100 samples from COD10K and 35 samples from CAMO as validation set, mixing the train and validation splits of the two datasets during training. This results in 3825 training and 135 validation samples. The testing samples are of size 1974 and 250, with 4121 additional zero-shot samples from NC4K.

EarthReason consists of 2,731, 1135, and 1928 training, testing and validation images with ~6 prompts per image. We take the full training and testing sets, and a sample of 500 unique images and prompts from the validation set to balance validation robustness with speed. We select checkpoints with the highest mean validation performance across gIoU and cIoU.

Challenging reasoning segmentation. In the challenging reasoning segmentation setting, in line with the state-of-the-art [66], we run a single-epoch first-stage VLM-only GRPO on InternVL3.5-8 on 10K samples from RefCocog [40], gRefCoco [28], and LVIS [16] without KL divergence and with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}. We use a global batch size of 16 unique prompts and a group size of 16 for a total of 256 generations per batch, and set the maximum output length to 2048. For the bootstrapping stage, our experience replay consists of 32 generation per group – double the amount compared to other trainings to minimize the number of groups with all-zero IoU. For our experiments after pretraining, we set the learning rates of both SAM3 and InternVL3.5-8B to 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, except for the second stage of B-GRTO, where SAM3’s learning rate is set to 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}. We train for 12 epochs. LoRA [19] is applied to the VLM with a rank of 64 across all stages and configurations.

ReasonSeg-X provides 240 training, 156 validation, and 773 test samples. ReasonSeg-R contains 968 test samples. We train and select checkpoints on its train/validation splits and benchmark on ReasonSeg-X and ReasonSeg-R test splits. We select checkpoints with the highest mean validation performance across the two metrics. We select checkpoints with the highest mean validation performance across gIoU and cIoU.

We run all experiments with a constant learning rate and zero weight decay, and divide summands within the GRPO objective in (3) by the fixed max output length, instead of by individual rollout length like in previous formulations [52], to avoid length bias [35]. We use the AdamW optimizer with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, and no learning-rate warmup or decay. We perform a single GRPO/GRTO gradient descent step on every sampled group.

Hyperparameter search. To identify strong training configurations, we first explore a small set of hyperparameter settings, summarized in Table 3. For each run, we perform a linear hyperparameter search starting from a default configuration: we vary one setting at a time, train for a few epochs, and monitor validation trends. We keep hyperparameters fixed when they are already established by a comparable baseline, such as in reasoning segmentation. One hyperparameter we observe plays a crucial role is gradient clipping: without gradient clipping, GRTO often collapses, so it is essential for stable joint training.

GRPO Reward. The GRPO reward is defined as

R=0.9​RIoU+0.1​Rformat.R=0.9\,R_{\mathrm{IoU}}+0.1\,R_{\mathrm{format}}. (16)

The IoU reward is computed from the final predicted mask M^final\hat{M}_{\mathrm{final}} and the binary ground-truth mask MM:

RIoU=|M^final∩M||M^final∪M|.R_{\mathrm{IoU}}=\frac{\left|\hat{M}_{\mathrm{final}}\cap M\right|}{\left|\hat{M}_{\mathrm{final}}\cup M\right|}. (17)

The format reward is an indicator for whether the language model produces a usable SAM prompt: it is equal to 1 only if InternVL3.5-8B outputs a valid, non-empty prompt that is successfully tokenized for SAM3; otherwise Rformat=0R_{\mathrm{format}}=0.

Segmentation loss. To fine-tune SAM3, we use BCE + soft-IoU loss. For each generated textual conditioning prompt, semantic head of SAM3 predicts a single foreground logit mask. The auxiliary objective combines pixel-wise binary cross-entropy with a soft overlap term: Let

S=σ⁡(M^)∈[0,1]H×W,S=\sigma(\hat{M})\in[0,1]^{H\times W},

where M^\hat{M} denotes the predicted semantic mask logits, SS is the corresponding soft mask probability, and M∈{0,1}H×WM\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} is the binary ground-truth mask. The semantic IoU-BCE auxiliary loss is

ℒsem=ℒBCE+ℒsIoU.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sIoU}}. (18)

The BCE term is

ℒBCE=−1H​W∑u=1H∑v=1W[Mu​vlogSu​v+(1−Mu​v)log(1−Su​v)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}=-\frac{1}{HW}\sum_{u=1}^{H}\sum_{v=1}^{W}\left[M_{uv}\log S_{uv}+(1-M_{uv})\log(1-S_{uv})\right], (19)

and the soft IoU term is

ℒsIoU=1−∑u=1H∑v=1WSu​v​Mu​v∑u=1H∑v=1W(Su​v+Mu​v−Su​v​Mu​v).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sIoU}}=1-\frac{\sum_{u=1}^{H}\sum_{v=1}^{W}S_{uv}M_{uv}}{\sum_{u=1}^{H}\sum_{v=1}^{W}\left(S_{uv}+M_{uv}-S_{uv}M_{uv}\right)}. (20)

This loss is averaged across the valid rollouts of the group: those where InternVL3.5-8B outputs a valid and non-empty prompt for SAM3.

Appendix G Prompts used

In this section, we provide the full prompts used to query InternVL3.5-8B across all three domains.

Remote sensing. We use the following template for the remote sensing domain, where "prompt" is replaced with the disentangled raw prompt as provided in the dataset.

Please find "{prompt}" with bbox(es). Also provide exactly one referential noun phrase that uniquely identifies the objects within the image. Return ALL matching instances; if there are no matches, return an empty answer (<answer></answer>). double-check none are missed. Output the bbox(es) of the interested object(s), along with a noun phrase, in JSON format. i.e., <answer>{"noun phrase": "a player in red", "objects": [[10,100,200,210], [225,296,706,786]]}</answer>

Camouflage detection. We use the following static prompt for the camouflage detection task. We omit the option to reject, change the provided example and include a "bbox" key in the JSON structure, as we observed that on this setting it leads to more consistent outputs for the baseline model.

Please find "Question" with bbox(es). Also provide exactly one referential noun phrase that uniquely identifies the objects within the image. Return ALL matching instances. double-check none are missed. Output the bbox(es) of the interested object(s), along with a noun phrase, in JSON format. i.e., <answer>"noun phrase": "brown mottled spider with bristly legs", "objects": ["bbox": [10,100,200,210], "bbox": [225,296,706,786]]</answer>

Challenging reasoning segmentation. We use the following prompt for setting if general-purpose complex reasoning, where "prompt" is replaced with the disentangled raw prompt as provided in the dataset. We explicitly instruct the model to perform iterative reasoning before providing a disentangled prompt.

Please find "{prompt}" with bbox(es). Also provide exactly one referential noun phrase that uniquely identifies the objects within the image. First, understand and summarize what the query -- "{prompt}"-- is likely referring to (which object or concept). Then apply this to the image and find the matched target object(s). Return ALL matching instances; if there are no matches, return an empty answer (<answer></answer>). double-check none are missed. Output the thinking process in <think> </think> and final answer in <answer> </answer> tags. Output the bbox(es) of the interested object(s), along with a noun phrase, in JSON format. i.e., <think> thinking process (step-by-step reasoning) here </think> <answer>"noun phrase": "a player in red", "objects": ["bbox": [10,100,200,210], "bbox": [225,296,706,786]]</answer>

Appendix H Existing assets, licenses, and terms of use

We use only existing datasets, pretrained models, and software assets. We cite the original papers for all datasets and models used in the main text. Below, we summarize the licenses and terms of use that we could verify from the corresponding official project pages, repositories, or model/dataset cards. When a license could not be verified from the official release page, we mark it as “not specified” rather than assuming a license.

  • •

    InternVL3.5-8B is a pretrained VLM used as the policy backbone πθ\pi_{\theta} for all experiments. Its license is Apache-2.0 according to the Hugging Face model card. The card also states that the Qwen3 component is licensed under Apache-2.0.

  • •

    SAM3 is a pretrained segmentation model used as the trainable segmentation tool ψω\psi_{\omega}. Its license is the Meta custom SAM License, covering model code, trained weights, inference code, training/fine-tuning code, and documentation.

  • •

    EarthReason is a dataset used for remote sensing segmentation training, validation, and testing. Its license is Apache-2.0 according to the Hugging Face dataset card.

  • •

    COD10K is a dataset used for camouflage detection training, validation, and testing. Its official COD10K/SINet release page permits non-commercial use only. We use it only for academic research.

  • •

    CAMO is a dataset used for camouflage detection training, validation, and testing. Its license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The official project page states that data and code are non-commercial and share-alike.

  • •

    NC4K is a dataset used for zero-shot camouflage detection testing. We could not verify an explicit license on the official release/download page. We therefore treat its license as not specified, use it only for academic evaluation, and cite the original dataset paper.

  • •

    ReasonSeg is a dataset used for zero-shot reasoning segmentation evaluation. We could not verify an explicit license on the LISA release page. We therefore treat its license as not specified, use it only for academic evaluation, and cite the original dataset paper.

  • •

    ReasonSeg-R is a dataset used for zero-shot reasoning segmentation evaluation. We could not verify an explicit license on the Hugging Face dataset card; the dataset card is empty. We therefore treat its license as not specified, use it only for academic evaluation, and cite the StAR paper.

  • •

    ReasonSeg-X is a dataset used for reasoning segmentation training, validation, and testing. The StAR code repository is Apache-2.0, but the Hugging Face ReasonSeg-X dataset cards we checked do not state an explicit dataset license. We therefore treat the dataset license as not specified and use it only for academic research.

  • •

    RefCOCOg is a dataset used for Stage-1 grounding pretraining for reasoning segmentation. The commonly used refer API is Apache-2.0. The data is based on MS COCO images; the original referring-expression annotation license is not explicitly specified in the API page we checked.

  • •

    gRefCOCO is a dataset used for Stage-1 grounding pretraining for reasoning segmentation. Its license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 / non-commercial research only according to the GRES/gRefCOCO project page.

  • •

    LVIS is a dataset used for Stage-1 grounding pretraining for reasoning segmentation. LVIS annotations and website are licensed under CC BY 4.0. LVIS images come from COCO and remain subject to COCO image terms.

  • •

    MS COCO images are the underlying images for RefCOCOg, gRefCOCO, and LVIS-derived data. COCO annotations are licensed under CC BY 4.0; COCO does not own the image copyrights, and image use must follow the corresponding Flickr terms and per-image licenses.

  • •

    StAR repository / ReasonSeg-X release code is the code and dataset release repository used for baseline comparison and as the ReasonSeg-X / ReasonSeg-R data source. The repository code is Apache-2.0. Dataset cards for the specific Hugging Face data releases do not state an explicit license.

All uses of non-commercial datasets in this paper are for academic research and benchmarking only. We do not redistribute the original datasets as part of this submission.
